title: Why Are Orcas Sinking Sailboats? Scientists Have a Wild Theory
summary:
Since 2020, a critically endangered group of fewer than 50 orcas has been ramming sailboats off the coasts of Spain and Portugal — and sometimes sinking them. The behavior continued into 2026. On July 23, orcas struck a sailboat named Idem repeatedly until it sank; the two people aboard were rescued. On August 29, a pod of four orcas broke off half the rudder of a 42-foot yacht. Less than 48 hours later, a Spanish rescue vessel had to escort another damaged yacht into port. The encounters kept coming through September.

So why are the whales doing this? Scientists aren't sure, but they have some intriguing ideas. One early guess — revenge — was quickly dismissed. In May 2024, experts suggested the behavior might be play. Atlantic bluefin tuna, the orcas' main food, have become more plentiful thanks to ocean protection rules. With more tuna around, the whales spend less time hunting, leaving young orcas with extra free time to explore. The scientists think the whales may see boat rudders as fun toys.

Another theory comes from biologist Bruno Díaz López and his team at Spain's Bottlenose Dolphin Research Institute. They propose that young orcas may be using boats to practice hunting skills. Tuna can grow 10 feet long and weigh hundreds of pounds, and they swim fast in large groups. Orcas work together to separate one fish, then chase it until it's exhausted. Sailboats move swiftly and quietly — much like tuna. "This is like a training toy," Díaz López said. "It's a shame that we humans are in the middle of this game, but they are learning."

Not everyone is happy. In early September, Spanish authorities reported that Toñi, the 60-year-old matriarch of the pod, had been shot with a pellet gun, leaving wounds on her dorsal fin. She appears to be healing. Scientists advise boaters to avoid areas where orcas are present, make loud banging noises to deter them, or replace smooth rudders with rougher ones to make boats less fun to play with.
why_it_matters: It shows that protecting a species can create brand-new conflicts, so the next generation will have to decide how people and intelligent wild animals share the same ocean and coastline.

background_read: Orcas, also called killer whales, are the largest members of the dolphin family and live in family groups called pods that are usually led by an older female.

The whales in this story belong to a small population living off the Iberian Peninsula — the corner of Europe shared by Spain and Portugal — near the Strait of Gibraltar, a narrow channel where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea.
That population is critically endangered, meaning it is at serious risk of dying out, and both Spain and Portugal protect it by law, so injuring an orca is illegal.
Researchers only began documenting these boat encounters in 2020; before that, incidents like them were essentially unheard of in the region.

Scientists know animals can pass new habits from one generation to the next — birds learning to open milk bottles, for instance — a process called cultural transmission, which helps explain how the behavior spread through this pod.

perspectives.description: Researchers see the behavior as evidence of how social and clever orcas are, and they point out that the tuna recovery behind it is a conservation success story worth celebrating.
Sailors say the encounters are frightening, costly and sometimes life-threatening; even when everyone is rescued, a sunken yacht is a serious loss.
They are alarmed that someone shot Toñi, the pod's matriarch. Hurting a critically endangered animal is illegal and could set back the recovery of a population with fewer than 50 members.
This fits a classic human–wildlife conflict pattern: when a protected species rebounds and shares space with people, new deterrents, boat designs and rules are needed to keep both sides safe.
